records.title: Show HN: I'm a dermatologist and I vibe coded a 3D biophysical skin model
records.author: sungam
records.storyText:
I'm a dermatologist. A year ago I posted a skin cancer quiz I vibe coded with Gemini 2.5 Pro. A top comment said that was the limit of vibe coding.

This year I tried something more ambitious: SkinLab, a biophysical model of human skin that runs in the browser using WebGL. You can cut it or wound it and it heals realistically to form a scar. Then you can treat the scar with laser and watch the healing process.

- 1.2 million voxels (0.25 mm resolution) for epidermis, dermis and fat. - Spring lattice with a J-shaped collagen fibre law and tension along the skin's lines - Healing as coupled ODEs (TGF-beta, myofibroblasts, collagen, contraction) - One static HTML file, WebGL, three.js, no backend

By accurate I mean the constants come from published papers and it reproduces biophysical behaviour, such as incisions opening more when made more across the skin's tension lines and offloading preventing raised scars. It is not validated against patient outcomes, so it's for research and teaching, and a small step towards my lab's long term goal of an accurate cellular-resolution model of human skin.

Built with Claude Code over five days. I guided the anatomy and biology through many rounds of feedback and iteration but I believe that in the future agentic models will be able to iteratively build and improve integrative models based upon analysis of published literature.

The tour (top right) takes a minute and runs in real time in your browser. Feedback welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Open-source skills for end-to-end video ad campaigns
records.author: sayonidroy
records.storyText:
Hey there! We are building SuperCMO Skills, open source tools which allow agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) to research, plan and create video and image campaigns end-to-end right out of your terminal or IDE.

We got tired of paying for expensive AI subscriptions and wasting countless hours assembling a pipeline for just one video ad, so we created these tools for ourselves. SuperCMO integrates with your agents to provide the ability to plan, shoot, edit, and stitch complete campaigns.

We began with simple prompt wrappers but soon realized the need to rethink our entire pipeline to overcome common limitations of the AI video.

- Pipeline Orchestration: Creating one ad now requires jumping through several apps: writing scripts in one, creating images in another, recording audio in yet another, and stitching the whole thing in an editor. SuperCMO does all of that natively. The tool knows how to choose the appropriate model (like automatically switching prompts for Veo versus Seedance) and do the whole post-production, including trimming and voiceover synchronization.

- Consistency from Shot to Shot: In true AI video generators, products and actors continually transform from shot to shot. We solved that problem by storyboarding before rendering and locking in master reference images in every generation.

- Directional Control: Completely automated agents often go awry creatively. So, we've developed the capabilities to take a peek at every stage of the process. You're always in control, approving the creator, the story idea, and the script before anything is expensively rendered.

People are using this today to create UGC product ads (give the agent a product photo and it chooses the creator, generates the script, and creates a ready MP4 file) or to analyze competitors' work (agent analyzes the winning advertisement from the competitor and recreates it with your product in mind).

This project will be released under an Apache-2.0 license. You can come to us with your own vendor keys to have everything done for free or to generate using our keys and just pay for each usage without any lock-in.

Thank you for your attention!

records.title: Show HN: Corral kill every command your agent starts
records.author: CG144
records.storyText:
This summer I got to intern on the backend of an AI agent and I noticed that it would run commands like tail -f or some random background jobs and exit without terminating any of these. I got curious and looked up how Claude Code handles stuff like this, and it turns out they have similar problems.

There are issues about background processes from the Bash tool not getting cleaned up when the session ends, and one where a timeout sends SIGTERM to the whole process group and ends up killing Claude Code itself. Most runners only kill the process they started, so anything that double forks, runs in the background, or keeps stdout open either survives or makes the runner hang.

Corral was me attempting to make a fix for this problem, while also trying to learn about processes and signals in Linux. You run corral --wall 30s -- yourcommand and by the time it's done, nothing it started should be running.

The command gets its own session so killing it can't kill you, and there's a mode where it runs in its own cgroup so the whole tree gets killed at once, including processes that may have changed sessions or process groups.

If there's no cgroup available it tracks the tree through /proc instead (this is a bit weaker, it still catches processes that changed sessions once their parent dies, but it can't kill anything running as a different user or anything handed off to another service like systemd), and if it can't confirm everything is dead it exits with 120.

Would love any feedback and more stuff along these lines i can do to learn more

records.title: Show HN: NetWasm – Independent .NET Compiler/Runtime (82.5 KB Hello World in C#)
records.author: zionsati
records.storyText:
I’ve been building NetWasm: an independent .NET compiler, CoreLib and runtime designed specifically for WebAssembly. It compiles Roslyn-generated CIL into standalone core WASM or WASI Preview 2 components - without shipping CoreCLR or Mono.

A clean Release application containing Console.WriteLine(42) produces 82.5 KB of final WASM with WASI p2, including the runtime and precise garbage collector.

Website: https://www.netwasm.com/ Playground: https://playground.netwasm.com/

The playground runs fully on the browser without a backend / cloud server compiling your code - it's all WASM! Locally, you use dotnet new, dotnet build, dotnet test, etc like you would normally. You can run the self-contained .wasm output with wasmtime, fully portable.

GitHub repos: https://github.com/zion-sati/NetWasm https://github.com/zion-sati/NetWasm.Libraries

What is it?

It's CIL (used to be called MSIL - it's the dotnet bytecode in other words) to WASM compiler. But more than that it's intentionally not using Microsoft's Corelib. We avoid reflection, typename with full namespace strings etc where the resulting .wasm can end up bloated. The goal is to have C# (and later .NET in general - thus F# and VB.NET) be on equal footing as Kotlin/WASM. Note that Kotlin/WASM uses WasmGC, NetWasm uses BoehmGC in precise mode. NetWasm makes Wasm a first class target.

Why NetWasm?

I fell in love with C# in 2006 and have OSS attempts at building C#-like syntax using C++ template metaprogramming with BoehmGC a long time ago because I didn't like the idea of having a runtime pre-installed. This idea was revitalized when I tried to migrate my web UI framework FUI-RS to C# - the resulting smoke test was already a minimum of 1 MB Brotli compressed running in interpreter mode! FUI-RS (Rust) had it at under 50 KB uncompressed. What already works?

C# 15, precise GC, finalization, exceptions, generics, virtual/interface dispatch, LINQ, tasks / value tasks (thus async-await), JSON, dependency injection, regex, XML, HTTP, WIT/WASI and TUnit (a modern source generated unit testing framework) etc.

What's left to do?

There's a roadmap to v1.0 on the repo's README - tl;dr there's a lot to do before we can get there, e.g. Expression trees, faster dev loops, threading, web workers, interop via libimport and globalization (opt-in just like NetWasm's implementation of timezone info).

NuGet packages should be able to multitarget to support NetWasm as well as the full .NET as long as there's no reflection / typename involved.

Licence: Runtime, CoreLib, templates and libraries: MIT Compiler and tooling: NetWasm Community License

Note that NetWasm is pre-1.0 (currently v0.5) and evolving rapidly, so I'd appreciate any technical feedbacks from the community if you'd like to help me shape this project. Particularly, real WASI use cases people want supported, NuGet packages to multitarget (or even better if you're one of the popular open source packages and would like to start multitargeting).

records.title: Show HN: CodeDiff – Fast (<100ms), robust (99.95%) syntax-aware code diff
records.author: FabCH
records.storyText:
Hi folks!

Because of AI, there is more code to review. I don't know about you, but I get annoyed when the default git diff doesn't match something "obvious". I built CodeDiff to help.

It's a syntax-aware, careful implementation in Rust of all current research in code diffing. It parses 24 languages with TreeSitter and falls back to a modified Myers line diffing algorithm for any file it cannot parse. I wouldn't necessarily call it a novel algorithm, but it isn't a re-implementation of existing tools either.

I tested it on the last 50 commits of all 7400-or-so repositories that are in the Gentoo package list. CodeDiff can diff 99.95% of those file pairs in 120s and 6GB of RAM on a rusty 11 year old Intel E3-1275 v5. The median speed is 7ms and 93% of files are diffed in under 100ms.

I also did a bit of hand solving and have a test dataset of 1400 hand solved diffs. CodeDiff is perfect on 70% and near-perfect on 90% of them. But accuracy is actually a complex thing to measure, because if you are only after the AST diff, then it is perfect 89% of the time. Deciding what to paint however is not an objective thing so if you do try it out, check out the render options (press M) and make it fit your style.

If you just want to see how it looks like: https://ivankovic.github.io/codediff/showcase/?case=python-r...

If you want to install it: https://github.com/ivankovic/codediff

Do feel free to file issues. It's v0.1.1 at the moment, but I have been using it for months as my git difftool and I plan to keep that stable. Using it as a library directly from Rust however, might change until v1.0. The final goal for v1.0 is p99 < 400ms and 99% perfect diff, including multi-file diff support in 30 languages.

Credit where credit is due: There is a bunch of people researching diffs in the past 20 or so years. Without those papers, CodeDiff would be a lot harder to build. Especially without APTED and Myers algorithms.

License: AGPL3.0, I kind of like copy-left. If your company prevents use of AGPL software tell them to throw a few bucks my way for my token usage and we can talk.

AI disclosure: I use AI assisted coding. Claude and Mistral were used, heavily.

records.title: Show HN: LogPhase – See a PR's blast radius as impacted user journeys
records.author: logphase
records.storyText:
Hi all,

I've been working on this app for a few months now, and I think it's at a stage where I can share it with everyone.

I built this app because AI-assisted coding is here to stay. With the right harness, AI can handle many things that were previously difficult. It can even perform PR reviews, in many ways better than humans. However:

> Code is only the visible part of a program. The real program is the understanding behind it: why it's built this way, how it maps to the business, and what breaks when you change it. That understanding lives in people, not in files.

Every day I slog through reviewing quite a few PRs containing dozens of file changes, and the only thing I had were file diffs. I struggled to build a complete picture of how all those different pieces connected. I'd jump between files and functions in my IDE, trying to piece together how they all fit.

So I built this tool to avoid hopping between different files and functions. You give it a PR, and it calculates the blast radius in the form of impacted or new user journeys. In those user journeys, you can see what was changed. You don't need to hop between different files, and for each step in the journey, you can go directly to the code. It provides full context in one single view.

A lot of the time I thought, "Okay, why do I need to build this thing? Claude can do it." Still, I was never happy with Claude's output, and I always found myself reaching for this tool. At some point I thought, "Why not just build it properly and share it with everyone?" This tool has helped me immensely with my understanding of the codebase.

Visualising code as a city is not the main goal of this tool, but I wanted to try it anyway. I think it's pretty cool. Sometimes, looking at the size, height, and width of a building gives me a feeling that maybe that class needs some refactoring.

I put a lot of effort into this. I do intend to sell it commercially, but before that, I wanted to see if people find it useful. Would love your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Investment Bets – market bets at live prices, humans or AI
records.author: php_survivor
records.storyText:
I've long been an index-investing type of person, but last year I started making some side bets, especially in tech (some inspired by WSB). I was sharing them with friends and wanted to simplify that.

This is how Investment Bets came about: you pick a ticker, a direction (long or short) and optionally a target date. The server fetches and records your entry price when you open the bet, and your exit price when you close it or reach the target date.

Each bet is scored on percentage gain/loss and has equal weight, so account size doesn't matter. The leaderboard sums your percentage results. I wanted to reward being right consistently, and since there's no compounding, a bad streak doesn't make your next good bets count for less.

The API is also open to AI agents. There's an OpenAPI file, llms.txt, Agent Skills under /.well-known and a single-file demo agent that reads headlines and places at most one bet per run. The checks that matter are in code (duplicate ticker, past target date, ticker the server can't resolve), so they don't depend on the model following the prompt. Agents get the same server-recorded prices as everyone else and show up on the same leaderboard.

https://investment-bets.com

https://investment-bets.com/agent

Please let me know if you have questions or feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Rename.Tools – Open-source bulk file renaming in the browser
records.author: wayne8848
records.storyText: Hi HN, I built Rename.Tools after needing to rename a large batch of images. This is something I only do occasionally, so I couldn’t justify buying dedicated software for it. The free tools I tried didn’t quite fit my needs either. When I discovered the File System Access API, a browser-based tool felt like a natural fit: open a tab when I need it, rename my files locally, and close it when I’m done. No installation or account required. The main feature is a chain of rename rules. You can combine find-and-replace, regex, sequential numbering, case conversion, text insertion, cleanup, and custom JavaScript, then drag them into the order you want. A live preview shows the resulting filenames and detects conflicts before you apply changes. There are also a few features for more specific workflows: - Rename photos using EXIF metadata and music files using audio tags. - Filter files by name, extension, size, or modification time. - Save reusable presets and import, export, or share them through a URL. - Undo renaming operations or export undo scripts. - Match TV episodes through TMDb, using your own API key. Files are processed locally and aren’t uploaded. The optional TMDb lookup requires network access. Direct renaming requires a supported Chromium browser. You can also export Bash or PowerShell scripts to run locally, including from browsers that don’t support direct renaming. There’s a sample mode if you’d like to try it without selecting your own files. The project is free and open source. I’d be interested to hear how you handle occasional bulk renaming, which workflows this is missing, and whether anything feels confusing. Try it: https://rename.tools/en/app Source: https://github.com/chenz24/rename.tools

records.title: Show HN: HankyDoodle – a Draw Something-style game I built with my kids
records.author: hankinsoft
records.storyText:
Hi. I'm a self-employed dev of ~15 years mainly known for my SQLPro products. Recently my kids have been getting into drawing and I wanted a game like the old DrawSomething which I used to play a ton. It no longer seems to exist, and the alternatives I tried either had 'watch this ad' or 'pay for coins' to unlock either tools or drawing colours.

HankyDoodle is a draw-and-guess game for iOS and Android. The main part I enjoyed working on was the file storage. I had to come up with a format for the drawing animations that had to be small but store enough information to be able to animate it at playback speeds. It also had to be practical to store and serve hundreds of thousands of them - right now I'm sitting at slightly less than 20,000 drawings. Currently, the drawing sizes are typically between 1 and 12kb.

Drawings are recorded as a stream of operations that include each stroke's tool, colour, points and timing. The format (a small RLE/palette/varint container) and the renderer are one C core, which gets shared + linked multiple ways. This makes sure the rendering is byte-identical across all platforms (iOS, Android and WebAssembly). Unfortunately I did mess up some of the code used for flood fills and if I don't render the image at the same size the drawings come out slightly differently (for that reason I render all drawings at one size then resize after when I need thumbnails). Luckily I did build a version system into the drawings, so it's something future me (sucker) can deal with at some point.

Drawings are stored in S3 and served via CloudFront. The backend is PHP and MySQL, but built in a way that I should be able to scale it out/replace it as needed.

Although it was not originally planned, it makes a pretty neat demo that you can navigate to the website and playback drawings as well. https://hankydoodle.app/d/01M37AKQF6MCRRXCHB3YSAVBVG is an example of one of the more detailed drawings by someone with way more talent than me. The app has a 'word of the day' feature where users can submit their own artwork and that's an example of an extremely detailed one.

Features of the game:

- 1v1 async drawing and guessing. You draw a picture. Your opponent guesses when they get the chance.

- A forever guess mode. If you don't want to draw you can just go in and guess drawings made by others. Drawings get 'released' into the forever guess pool once a user has guessed the drawing.

- A word of the day where anyone can take a crack at drawing the word.

- A showcase where the best drawings can be found.

- Offline drawing, where you can draw while offline and without any sort of signup.

- A 'doodlepedia' where you can try and draw every word.

- An online portfolio of your drawings (such as https://hankydoodle.app/u/TP1N34).

- Privacy mode, where your drawings are private and only the folks you draw with can see them.

- Family mode where certain drawings and words get filtered completely out of your view.

The app has an unobtrusive banner ad which can be removed via a $3.99USD/year subscription. I know people don't like subscriptions, but that was the best alternative I could come up with and still keep the app free to most while covering my costs.

Happy to go deep on the format, the renderer, the fill, or the solo-dev tradeoffs.

records.author: charlesabarnes
records.storyText:
Howdy HN! I'm Charles and I wanted to share something I am working on right now: gangway (https://gangway.sh/).

Gangway is a simple way to quickly spin up ephemeral containers for previews, demos, artifacts, and temporary sharing

This app has started months ago as an idea to take advantage of spare compute capacity I have and to keep some of my hosting costs down. Initially I tried PaaS apps such as Coolify and Dokku, but it didn't provide a way for me to quickly and easily distribute apps I write by hand. Then, I tried creating a few prototypes and failing due to them being overly complex or broad scoped.

What I landed on was built one feature at a time:

- PR previews - This provided immediate utility to me for my frontend work. I get to review my teams code without being woried about usage or billing

- UI to quickly spin up a preview environment - If I have something I want to show a client but it isn't ready to go live on their domain yet, I can drag in a folder, let gangway figure out how to run it, optionally protect it with a password then send them a personalized URL.

- MCP - I thought it would be even easier if I can have an LLM deploy the app at any time without much thought. I have used this to message and quickly remedy and preview a bug fix from my phone before it shipped out.

- Artifacts - After adding the MCP I realized I often wanted my agent to generate visualizations or previews of features before implementation. Claude users may recognize the general idea from Artifacts, except these can be full stack apps you control.

Some examples currently running on gangway, all created from short conversations with different agents:

- Paged at 2 am - a user flow for a web-app on a canvas: https://paged-at-2am.demo.gangway.sh

- A slide deck from one markdown file (an artifact): https://four-day-week.demo.gangway.sh

- Bottle Sea, a small Bun + Postgres app: https://bottle-sea.demo.gangway.sh

- Quickfire Trivia - multiplayer rooms: https://quickfire-trivia.demo.gangway.sh

- A black hole: https://event-horizon.demo.gangway.sh

- FLUX a multiplayer physics demo: https://flux.demo.gangway.sh

Install is a one-liner or a quick docker compose setup (https://github.com/charlesabarnes/gangway#quickstart), and there's a local-only mode with cloudflare quick tunnel links if you don't want to expose anything.

I am considering deploying a multi-tenant hosted version of this to make it even easier. Let me know of any feedback that you may have!

records.title: Show HN: Search2o – Search that finds and runs an AI agent for each request
records.author: ramvenkat11
records.storyText:
I have been working on search systems for a while, and I always wondered: What if search, instead of matching documents, matched workflows and ran those workflows?

I called it “Search that executes” — as opposed to search that retrieves information.

When AI agents showed up a few years ago, I realized that those workflows could be agents — capable of understanding a user’s query and taking branches dynamically. That’s when I got excited enough about the idea to implement it.

To make this work, it needs more than just search: a structured framework for defining agents (so the system “understands”), a controlled runtime for executing them with guardrails, and an end-to-end system with a UI to request and receive user approval before taking critical actions.

It made sense that all this plumbing should be handled behind the scenes, letting programmers concentrate on the agent’s business logic. Many design decisions followed directly from that.

Agents are created in a JSON structure. There are 23 “commands” that define the units of work an agent performs. Python expressions can be used in strings within curly braces.

Because the whole thing has a structure/schema, AI generates valid agents from English descriptions: “Create a RAG agent to call the company purchase order system”, “Create a tool-calling agent to …”. You can check this out in the live demo on the website.

The developer creates an agent, describes it in plain English, and publishes it in the system. Users just submit a request. Search matches the request to an agent, and the system runs the agent. The demo also shows searching for and executing agents.

That’s the central idea. The website has more information on other aspects. Despite the enterprise-y look and feel of the website, the system was really created by just me over the last couple of years. I would love to answer any questions and hear your comments and feedback.

records.storyText:
Hello, Caffold is an open-source, self-hosted workspace for coding agents. You can continue the same work across desktop, foldable, tablet, and phone.

I started building it for myself in late June. It was initially only for Codex. I got a Galaxy Z Fold8 in early August and started using Caffold much more seriously. By late August, I had moved my existing Codex work into Caffold too. I've been doing all of my development work in Caffold since then. After about a month of that, it finally feels ready to share. For now, it supports the three agents I actually use day to day: Codex, Claude Code, and Grok.

The idea came from how my work had changed. Coding agents now write almost all of the code. I spend most of my time reading code and diffs, watching what the agents are doing, steer them when needed, and give the next instruction.

When I saw the upcoming Fold8, its unfolded screen looked large enough for this kind of work. I rarely need to type code myself. I often enter prompts by voice as well as with a keyboard. So I started wondering if a foldable could be my main interface for development rather than just a secondary device.

I also wanted to see how far I could go with the browser platform itself. The frontend is plain JavaScript and CSS. It uses Web Components and native ES modules. There is no TypeScript, React/Vue/Svelte, or bundler. (That doesn't mean I avoid external libraries entirely. I use things like xterm.js and pdf.js where they make sense.)

I'm also curious how many people will want to use foldables this way, especially now that devices like the iPhone Duo are coming too.

records.title: Show HN: Assay – a QA CLI that finds bugs with no LLM and no tests written
records.author: awss1i
records.storyText:
I've always found it odd there was no deterministic QA tools with zero baseline needed, especially after so long. It's always been either (1) playwright or cypress that require written tests, dependant on the tests YOU write, or (2), asking the LLM to find and test bugs in your code, which has 2 cons, its costly (sometimes), and its non-deterministic.

That's why i built assay. Its only dependencies is playwright & chromium, and you point it at any folder with a webpage and it runs tests on its own by driving the webpage itself in a browser and clicking every control.

It then flags anywhere the webpage contradicted/disagreed with itself; it doesn't know right from wrong NOR what the webpage is about, but universally, a page disagreeing with itself is almost always a bug.

An example of this is on a paint app, if you draw two strokes on a canvas and click undo twice, you expect them both to undo each stroke sequentially; in one of 225 benchmarks, clicking the undo the first time didn't remove the first stroke, and only the 2nd click worked. assay drove that and caught it.

As for benchmarks, there are 2 variants that are all reproducible in the repo. The first is 225 generated web pages that were first checked by hand, then had assay run on them. There was a total of 20 bugs across all programs, and assay caught 15 with the right reasoning, and had 0 false failures. The second was a harder one where an LLM planted 5 bugs across 10 working original webpages. assay found 12 of the 50 and had 0 false failures, which may seem low, but assays superpower is that its cheap and quick.

assays median runtime is 14s, and it plugs into 15 agentic coding harnesses with a skill, plus claude code and deepseek harness have their own plugin that automatically runs it with a stop hook every time the LLM touches a webpage.

My favourite feature is that it groups flagged tests together if their of the same bug. More details are in the repo about this since this is getting a little long, but the links it makes have its own benchmarks, 51/51 links it got right with 0 false links. This serves as additional context to you, if you use it as a raw cli, or to your agent if your using it with an LLM harness.

pip install assay-ui. All alternative methods to install are on the github, including harness support.
